records.name: Soccsksargen
records.current_summary: In June 2025, transgender-rights activist Ali Jejhon Macalintal was shot dead in General Santos City. Human Rights Watch called the killing an “apparent targeted killing” and said police were examining her activism as a possible motive. The national Commission on Human Rights publicly condemned the killings of two transgender women as “marked by cruelty and impunity” — the strongest official wording in this record for any region — and named Macalintal.  No protective ordinance or institutional counterweight is documented in this region, and the killing stood unresolved as of the record's sources. For a trans visitor the finding is targeted lethal violence against activists in a province with an official acknowledgement of impunity and no local machinery to answer it.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch statement (June 2025) on the murdered trans-rights activist in the Philippines: Macalintal's General Santos shooting as an apparent targeted killing and police examining her activism as a motive. (Record URL is a rewritten, 404-returning variant of the cited HRW address and the cached copy captured only site navigation; content per the research dossier.)

Philippine daily report (27 June 2025): the Commission on Human Rights condemns the killings of two transgender women as marked by cruelty and impunity, naming Macalintal. (Publisher returns HTTP 403 to automated fetch; summary from the research dossier line.)

Bulatlat report (Dominic Gutoman, 26 June 2025): on 23 June 2025 an unidentified gunman killed trans woman and former journalist-activist Ali Macalintal inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos City; Macalintal was a former deputy secretary general of Karapatan-Soccsksargen Region and a former anchor-reporter of Radio Philippines Network DXDX-General Santos City. Bahaghari decried the killing and also reported the earlier killing of trans woman Shalani Dolina in Caloocan, and the piece notes no national anti-discrimination statute exists, with the SOGIESC Equality Bill stuck in Congress for 25 years. Region-naming source that independently confirms the General Santos City killing and Macalintal's own Soccsksargen-based activism role that this record's summary claims.

Rappler MovePH piece (3 July 2025): during Pride Month the Commission on Human Rights called the string of killings of transgender women a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide', citing human rights advocate Ali Macalintal being shot inside an acupuncture clinic (General Santos) alongside 18-year-old student Kierra Apostol and the earlier gunning down of beauty salon owner Ren Tampus; groups used the killings to push the Simplified Legal Gender Recognition Bill, with CHR's Fayda M. Dumarpa pledging support. Major-media confirmation that the Macalintal killing in General Santos is officially framed as part of a national transfemicide pattern, corroborating this record's claim of official acknowledgement without a protective institutional answer.

records.name: Calabarzon
records.current_summary: This region surrounds the national capital without sharing its protective ordinances: none is documented here, and the visitor picture is the national one — killings of trans women without dependable local machinery.  Against that backdrop, in August 2025 a newly crowned LGBTQ pageant winner was found dead with 13 stab wounds in a city south of the capital, days after the crowning, and police worked the killing as a homicide case — a high-signal violent episode for this region's record.

sources.claim: Philippine daily report (13 August 2025): LGBTQ pageant winner murdered in Batangas — the Lipa City finding with 13 stab wounds days after the crowning, worked as a homicide case. (Publisher returns HTTP 403 to automated fetch; summary from the research dossier line.)

Wikipedia's Philippines country overview documents the national framework behind this region's record: there is no national anti-discrimination law - the SOGIE Equality Bill has been proposed since the 2000s and failed to pass, and in November 2022 the newly elected government rejected United Nations recommendations including passage of the bill as "unacceptable" - and transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender. The page lists local anti-discrimination ordinances, several inside Calabarzon: Batangas province (2015), Cavite (2014-2018, later extended to cover gender identity), Batangas City (2016) and Calamba (2017), and it records that murders of transgender and gender-nonconforming persons in the Philippines have been reported since at least 2012.

records.name: ARMM
records.current_summary: In the Bangsamoro autonomous region justice is legally plural: the region's 2019 administrative code provides that it be dispensed in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, and traditional or tribal laws (the clause is carried in the research dossier; the cached code excerpt does not reach it), while the national Code of Muslim Personal Laws of 1977 remains in force. In July 2026 the Bangsamoro parliament tabled a bill for a comprehensive Shari'ah justice system code extending to ta'zir criminal offences — the category under which morality offences are prosecuted in comparable systems. No source establishes that Philippine Shari'ah courts currently prosecute same-sex conduct or gender expression, and no such law has yet passed.  The Shari'ah court system is expanding nationally: three new judicial districts and twelve circuit courts beyond BARMM were created by law signed in August 2024, extending into majority-Christian areas, with further access legislation in September 2025 and a Supreme Court resolution in January 2026 to operationalise the Shari'ah High Court.  The finding for a trans visitor is structural rather than enforcement-based: a dispute could fall outside the civil courts altogether, in a jurisdiction actively legislating criminal religious law with no protective ordinance or civil-rights infrastructure documented in the region. Forward-looking, and bounded by the fact that the ta'zir code is a proposal, not a power in force.

sources.claim: Full text of Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13 (the Bangsamoro Administrative Code), begun 29 March 2019, from the Bangsamoro Official Gazette: prescribes the structures and rules of governance of the autonomous region (cached extract covers the introductory provisions; the code's justice-dispensation clause — 'in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws' — is cited in the dossier), while guaranteeing religious freedom.

Bangsamoro Parliament (2026-07-14): proposed Shari'ah Justice Code — 10 books extending Shari'ah jurisdiction beyond the personal-status law confined since PD 1083 (1977) into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and ADR; rests on BOL authority and the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. For the record: marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums with written-opt-in clauses for civil entities — the legal-pluralist marriage regime a visitor's Muslim spouse-status questions would run through.

Christianity Today (2024-11): August 2024, President Marcos Jr. signed a law creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts, expanding the Shari'ah court system beyond the Bangsamoro into majority-Christian northern Mindanao, Davao-region provinces, parts of the Visayas, Luzon and Metro Manila; parliament passed it unanimously. For the record: dated confirmation that Bangsamoro's Shari'ah personal-law regime is expanding nationally, with local Christian-leader reaction.

freshness.fact: Code of Muslim Personal Laws (PD 1083, 1977) still in force per lawphil (page live); no repeal recorded; cited in Bangsamoro legal-pluralism context.

records.name: CAR
records.current_summary: In the Cordillera administrative region, inter-tribal customary justice runs alongside the formal system: the Kalinga bodong/pagta peace-pact system — with its own holders, sanctions and authority over crimes and tribal-related offences — was codified in February 2026 by the provincial government into a 137-page written Pagta, a step its sponsors present as recognition by the national courts. Academic documentation frames this as legal pluralism in which customary resolution of criminal and tribal offences operates with police, prosecutors and local officials participating, and constitutional recognition of indigenous justice extends across the country's autonomous regions.  No trans-specific bodong ruling, customary exclusion or punishment relating to gender expression appears in this record. The finding for a visitor is structural uncertainty — which forum decides a dispute — without any evidence of a trans-specific adverse outcome: the customary system here is a civil and restorative-justice institution with no criminal-law expansion over morality documented, which keeps it a marginal concern, not a threat finding.

sources.claim: Academic journal article on the bodong/pagta customary justice system in Kalinga: framed in legal-pluralism and restorative-justice theory, it documents bodong holders resolving criminal and tribal offences alongside the formal justice system, with Philippine National Police personnel, prosecutors and barangay officials participating in customary-law conflict resolution.

Wikipedia's article on Kalinga, a landlocked province within the Cordillera Administrative Region whose capital Tabuk was established when it was formed out of Kalinga-Apayao on 8 May 1995 by Republic Act No. 7878, documents the province as a long-standing flashpoint between the Marcos martial-law government (declared September 1972) and its indigenous peoples over the Chico River Dam Project, which would have displaced about 100,000 indigenous people, with the 24 April 1980 murder of tribal leader Macli-ing Dulag turning public opinion and making the dam dispute a landmark ancestral-domain case study in the country. It records the September 1986 Mount Data Peace Accord that created the Cordillera Autonomous Region and notes that attempts to ratify actual autonomy failed in plebiscites. For this record it frames the province's indigenous governance context in which the customary bodong/pagta justice system the summary concerns operates; it does not itself discuss the bodong/pagta codification.

Wikipedia's region framework page for the jurisdiction itself: the Cordillera Administrative Region was created on 15 July 1987, comprises six provinces (Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Kalinga and Mountain Province) centred on Baguio, is the country's only landlocked region and, per the 2020 Census of Population and Housing, the least populated in the country with fewer residents than the national capital. It describes the region as home to numerous ethnic groups, including a majority-Igorot province, and records a living Cordillera autonomy movement alongside the earlier Cordillera People's Liberation Army ceasefire secured by the Aquino government. A framework document for the jurisdiction in which the record's customary-justice claims sit, with the region itself as the subject.

freshness.fact: Codification of the Kalinga 'Pagta'/bodong peace-pact system confirmed (launched Feb 2026) but the cited bworldonline article now 404s; replaced by contemporaneous coverage.

records.name: Daegu
records.current_summary: Daegu has hosted the country's second-oldest queer culture festival every year since June 2009 — organisers mark seventeen consecutive years 'without fail', run 'as a form of resistance against hate and discriminatory politics', the 2025 edition under the slogan 'We Will Not Be E(r)ased' on central Daegu's Dongseong-ro. Organisers cite a Supreme Court ruling on local anti-discrimination ordinances as confirming sexual minorities as citizens protected by the Constitution.  The festival draws a recurring, organised counter-mobilisation: in September 2025 a Daegu–Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer', gathering roughly 3,500 believers from some 1,600 churches from Banwoldang station along a 450-metre stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans, timed against the festival. For a visible trans visitor the result is a concentrated confrontational environment during festival week; the event itself continues to take place annually despite interference.

sources.claim: Korea JoongAng Daily (2025-09): Daegu Queer Culture Festival has run every year since June 2009 without fail; the 2025 edition drew an injunction bid from the Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasure Committee, dismissed by the court — as were the 2022-24 bids — while police again restricted the march to a single bus-only lane and organizers framed the event as resistance to 'hate and discriminatory politics'. 2023, under then-Mayor Hong Joon-pyo, municipal officials physically blocked the road. For the record: the sharpest local hostility in South Korea — state-adjacent opposition recurring annually but judicially contained each time.

Kidok (Korean Christian daily, September 2025): a Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer' response to the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450 m stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans.

Wikipedia's article on the Daegu Queer Culture Festival (DQCF), the festival at the centre of this record: it has been held every year since 2009 as the country's second-largest LGBT event, a pride parade and film festival lasting a week or two and usually taking place in late June, and it faces standing opposition from religious groups, with an estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups forming a 'gay issue countermeasure committee' in Daegu to block LGBT events. The page records that such opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central Daegu street, and it carries survey context on national attitudes (Pew Research Center: 18% of South Koreans felt homosexuality should be tolerated in 2007, rising to 39% in 2013). Framework source confirming the record's claim of an annual festival since 2009 and a recurring, organised counter-mobilisation in Daegu.

No Cut News (English, 8 June 2026): the Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters — comprising the Daegu–Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association — filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea (NHRCK) demanding a change of venue for the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, claiming the event is likely to infringe on public welfare; the group says about 34,000 people signed, which it calls unusually large for a single NHRCK petition. The petition cites the Daegu District Court's dismissal of the festival committee's injunction request, a ruling that found the police notice restricting the event legitimate because Daegu's Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be secured for public welfare. It counteracts the festival committee's January petition against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act. Dated court-and-petition evidence that official venue restriction and organised anti-queer mobilisation over the festival continued into the 2026 edition, directly supporting this record's account of a confrontational environment around the event.

records.name: Daejeon
records.current_summary: In October 2021 the Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the Army's forced discharge of transgender soldier Byun Hee-soo, holding the military should have considered her a woman when reviewing fitness for duty — a ruling widely described as a landmark in the case brought to repeal the discharge decision.  On 24 June 2024, after the Ministry of National Defense reversed the Army's original 'natural death' classification and recognised the 2021 death as service-related, Byun was interred at the National Cemetery in Daejeon. Around 60 activists gathered to protest the burial, arguing her service did not qualify her for interment there: state recognition of a trans person at the national memorial ground, met with a small but public rejection in open space.

sources.claim: Yonhap (2021-10-07): Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the Army's discharge of the late Ssg. Byun Hee-soo — the first known legal case involving a transgender soldier — holding the military should have treated her as female after her legal sex change, that loss of genitalia was not valid grounds for dismissal, and that fitness review should weigh basic rights. Decision vindicated the posthumous appeal. For the record: dated, court-level proof that a Daejeon court delivered a pro-recognition ruling on trans military status.

Aju Press (2024-06-25): Korea's first transgender soldier Byun Hee-soo was buried at the National Cemetery in Daejeon on 24 June 2024 — some 60 activists protested, arguing the burial was marred by discriminatory treatment; she died by suicide in 2021 after the forced 2020 discharge (gender dysphoria classified as mental disorder, post-surgery physical-disability finding) and court appeals. For the record: her Daejeon state burial stands as official honouring contrasted with the still-conservative institutional stance.

records.name: Gyeonggi
records.current_summary: The model student human-rights ordinance covering discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity was first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province; Seoul's office adopted it in 2012 and it spread to other regional offices before the 2024–26 repeal wave.  When Seoul's metropolitan council — pushed by a campaign begun by religious and parents' coalitions in August 2022 — abolished the capital's ordinance on 26 April 2024, Gyeonggi stood among only six regional education offices still enforcing comparable ordinances, and a Gyeonggi-based teacher warned that wholesale abolition 'will bring a regression to human rights in the education sector'. The province's standing is thus origin-and-retention of student protections rather than any enforcement measure aimed at visitors.

sources.claim: Korea Times report (28 April 2024) on the Seoul Metropolitan Council's abolition of the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance twelve years after the Seoul office adopted it: the ordinance model was 'first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province'; abolition was pushed by the ruling People Power Party council after an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to its sexual-orientation clause; six regional education offices - Gyeonggi, Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju - still enforced comparable ordinances at publication; the (Seoul) superintendent began a sit-in protest against the abolition, and the opposition-led National Assembly said it would legislate a national student-rights act regardless of regional decisions. A quoted Gyeonggi-based teacher defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition.

The English Wikipedia article on South Korea's student human rights ordinances records that the framework 'first began in Gyeonggi-do Province (2010)' and that the Gyeonggi-do and Seoul ordinances are the only two to include the right not to be discriminated against on the basis of pregnancy, the Gyeonggi ordinance also covering sexual orientation and gender identity - the provisions most disputed in the 2024-26 repeal wave. It adds that in Gyeonggi-do the Superintendent of Public Instruction conducts an annual survey on student human rights and that Gyeonggi-do dedicates a day to Student Human Rights Day. The article corroborates this record's origin claim that Gyeonggi enacted the model ordinance first, in 2010, with sexual-orientation and gender-identity non-discrimination among its protections.

records.name: Bayern
records.current_summary: Since 1 April 2024, gender-inclusive German has been prohibited in schools, universities and all state administration in Bavaria, implementing the Söder government declaration of December 2023 through a cabinet decision amending the language rules of public authorities. Coverage notes critics dismissing the measure as symbol politics while recording its practical reach across every public counter, registry office and classroom a visitor might deal with.  Bavaria is also a partner — with Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt — in a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG) on legal gender change: an organised state-level attempt to make the nationwide self-ID law stricter, which critics see as restricting how trans and intersex people use the right.

sources.claim: Tagesschau report on Bavaria's gender-language ban: from 1 April 2024, gender-inclusive German is prohibited in schools, universities and all state administration, implementing the Söder government declaration of December 2023 and a cabinet decision amending the language rules of public authorities; critics in the coverage dismiss it as symbol politics while noting its practical reach across every public counter, registry office and classroom.

Antenne Bayern report on the Bundesrat initiative by several Länder — Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt, with Bavaria a partner — to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG) on legal gender change, i.e. an organised Land-level attempt to make the nationwide self-ID law stricter.

National framework page applying to Bavaria. Adults have been able to change legal gender since 1980; the Self-Determination Act (Cabinet-approved August 2023; Bundestag vote 374-251 on 12 April 2024) lets adults over 18 change first name and gender by self-determination with three months' notice, in force since 1 November 2024. Same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since 2017, and discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity is banned nationwide in employment and goods/services, though the page notes some protections vary by region. Supplies the federal legal baseline inside which Bavaria's own measures (the gender-language ban and the Länder push to tighten the SBGG) operate.

German Wikipedia article on the Self-Determination Act (SBGG), the federal law Bavaria's Bundesrat initiative sought to tighten. It passed the Bundestag on 12 April 2024 (374-251, 11 abstentions) and the Bundesrat on 17 May 2024, was gazetted 21 June 2024; changes could be registered from 1 August 2024 and took effect 1 November 2024. Adults declare the change themselves before the registry office; 14-17 year-olds need a guardian's (or the family court's) consent; for under-14s only the guardian can declare, and a three-month waiting period applies with a one-year lockout after a change. The article also records the Bundesrat's 20 October 2023 criticism that the draft let parents decide under-14 gender-entry changes 'without any counselling, examination and investigation of the child's welfare' - exactly the contested point behind the Bavarian-led tightening initiative this record covers.

records.name: Berlin
records.current_summary: Germany's Pride movement faces a documented rise in attacks: the amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-motivated attacks on Pride events nationally in 2024 and 30 in 2025 across roughly 120 parades, including a boiling-water attack, and runs a €100,000 support fund weighted to eastern Germany. Ahead of the 2025 Christopher Street Day, with hundreds of thousands expected, Berlin's organisers nonetheless urged participants to 'be vigilant'.  The reporting also situates the capital: Maneo, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, states that big-city parades like Berlin's had not been specifically threatened — smaller towns are hardest to police — while everyday hostility still surfaces: one Berlin-Neukölln queer café owner reports 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in eighteen months.

sources.claim: The Guardian (26 July 2025) on German Pride parades facing a rise in attacks: Berlin CSD organisers urge vigilance with hundreds of thousands expected; the amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-extremist attacks on Pride events nationally in 2024 and 30 so far in 2025 across ~120 parades (including an attack with boiling water), and runs a €100,000 CSD support fund focused on eastern Germany; Maneo, the Berlin anti-violence documentation project, states big-city parades like Berlin and Cologne were not specifically threatened and that smaller towns are hardest to police; a Berlin-Neukölln queer café owner reports 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months.

MANEO, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, states that it recorded 723 LSBTIQ+-hostile incidents in Berlin in 2025, slightly fewer than the 738 documented in 2024, from 1,014 new reports - a new high; its 12 May 2026 release lists insults, threats and physical attacks in public transport, parks and streets, with Schöneberg, Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Tiergarten most affected, plus 58 attacks on LSBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events. MANEO says the figures capture only part of reality because of a high dark figure, and that the counselling centre itself was attacked several times in 2025. This is the primary Berlin project behind the record's claim that documented homophobic violence in the capital is rising, and it names Neukölln - the record's café-owner example - among the worst-hit districts.

MANEO reports that at the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day a vehicle drove into a crowd in the Tiergarten area, killing one woman, injuring several people and forcing the event to be cancelled; the project offers victim counselling and an anonymous reporting line (030-2163336, daily 17:00-19:00). This is a dated, outcome-specific Berlin Pride incident - evidence that the serious attack risk the record's 2025 'be vigilant' organisers warned about has materialised at the capital's own CSD.

The Berlin state government's official prison-service page states that legislation has created a basis for considering trans, inter* and non-binary people held in custody, that Berlin prison staff are responsible for taking each detainee's individual needs into account within the legal framework, and it details gender-segregated placement, intake procedures and counselling and support offers. This is Berlin-specific official information on how the capital's prison administration (JVA Moabit, JVA für Frauen Berlin, etc.) treats trans/inter/non-binary detainees, the detention-side counterpart to the city's anti-queer violence statistics.

records.name: Brandenburg
records.current_summary: In Cottbus on 20 October 2025, a rubbish container was set alight against the façade of the 'Regenbogenkombinat' queer cultural centre during CSD week; the fire was out in about fifteen minutes and nobody was hurt, but state security (Staatsschutz) took over the arson investigation and a political motive cannot be excluded — local initiatives call it an attempted firebombing, and the attack sits among earlier suspected far-right attacks in the city.  The subsequent Cottbus CSD — the 17th edition, under the motto 'Vereint in Frieden und Vielfalt' — ran with a large police presence against two registered far-right counter-demonstrations, one organised by 'Deutsche Jugend voran', and proceeded without major disruption. The local queer community describes itself as unusually watchful: repeated physical pressure on infrastructure, met by a functioning protective response.
